Nai TalimSantiniketan and Visva-BharatiSwaraj and swadeshiUniversal humanism

Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore, whom Gandhi addressed as "Gurudev", rejected colonial, bookish education and worked for India's freedom, yet differed in emphasis. Gandhi's Nai Talim built education around a productive craft and self-reliant villages; Tagore's Santiniketan stressed freedom, nature and creativity. On nationalism, Gandhi led a mass movement for swaraj through swadeshi and non-cooperation, while Tagore warned against the cult of the nation and argued for universal humanism.

1. Common ground

  • Critique of colonial education: both attacked the English-medium, examination-driven system that produced clerks cut off from Indian life.
  • Mother tongue and learning by doing: both wanted teaching in the mother tongue, close to nature and village life.
  • Rural reconstruction: Gandhi's constructive programme and Tagore's Sriniketan (1922) both linked education to village welfare.

2. Differences in education

  • Aim: Gandhi stressed character, self-reliance and the dignity of labour, an education of "hand, head and heart"; Tagore sought the free and complete growth of the personality through art, music and imagination.
  • Method: the Wardha Scheme of Basic Education (1937), drafted by the Zakir Husain Committee, made a craft such as spinning or farming the centre of the curriculum, with schools partly paying for themselves; at Santiniketan (1901) classes were held under trees, with music, painting and festivals and no rigid syllabus.
  • Outlook: Gandhi's school was rooted in the village and national self-sufficiency; Tagore's Visva-Bharati (1921), whose motto means "where the world makes a home in a single nest", brought together scholars of East and West.
  • Science and machines: Gandhi was wary of machinery (Hind Swaraj, 1909); Tagore welcomed modern science.

3. Differences in nationalism

  • Gandhi: nationalism as mass, non-violent action: satyagraha, swadeshi, boycott, and the charkha as a symbol of self-reliance. It was not narrow: he wanted the cultures of all lands to blow freely through his house but refused to be blown off his feet by any (Young India, 1921).
  • Tagore: an early voice of the Swadeshi movement (1905), he grew wary of its coercion (Ghare Baire, 1916). His Nationalism lectures (1917) called the Western nation-state a machine of power and greed, and he renounced his knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh (1919).
  • The 1921 debate: in "The Call of Truth" Tagore questioned the burning of foreign cloth and blind obedience; Gandhi replied in "The Great Sentinel" (Young India, October 1921), defending spinning and non-cooperation as duties of the hour. Tagore returned to the theme in "The Cult of the Charka" (1925).
  • Reason and faith: when Gandhi called the Bihar earthquake (1934) a divine chastisement for untouchability, Tagore objected to linking a natural event with sin.

The two were complementary rather than opposed: Gandhi gave nationalism a mass base and a moral method, and Tagore guarded it against narrowness. Both live on in NEP 2020's stress on the mother tongue, vocational skills and the arts, and in an inclusive, humane nationalism.

Judicial independenceSeparation of powersBasic structureRule of law

Judicial independence means that judges decide cases free from pressure by the executive, the legislature, private interests or the passing public mood. The Constitution secures it through the method of appointment, security of tenure, financial autonomy and the separation of the judiciary from the executive (Article 50), and the Supreme Court has held it to be part of the basic structure (Fourth Judges case, 2015). Democracy is not mere majority rule; it is the rule of law with protected rights, which only an independent judiciary can guarantee.

1. Why independence is a prerequisite of democracy

  • Guardian of rights: Fundamental Rights are real only if courts can rule against the State. Article 32, which Dr Ambedkar called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, lets citizens move the Supreme Court directly; in Maneka Gandhi (1978) and Puttaswamy (2017) the Court protected liberty and privacy against executive power.
  • Check on majorities: judicial review keeps Parliament within the Constitution; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Minerva Mills (1980) protected the basic structure from passing majorities.
  • Integrity of elections: courts hear election petitions and have strengthened voters' rights, from candidates' disclosure of criminal records and assets (2002) to striking down electoral bonds (2024).
  • Federal umpire: the Supreme Court settles Centre–State disputes (Article 131) and, in S.R. Bommai (1994), curbed the misuse of President's Rule.
  • Equality before law: an impartial forum where the citizen and the State stand as equals is the essence of the rule of law.

2. Lessons from history

  • When independence weakened: the supersession of senior judges in appointing Chief Justices (1973, 1977) and ADM Jabalpur (1976), which denied detenus any remedy during the Emergency, showed how a pliant judiciary hollows out democracy.
  • Restoration: the Second and Third Judges cases (1993, 1998) created the collegium, Puttaswamy (2017) overruled ADM Jabalpur, and in 2015 the Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (99th Amendment) 4:1, holding that executive participation in appointments threatened independence.

3. Independence must come with accountability

  • Concerns: an opaque collegium, delays because the Memorandum of Procedure is still not finalised, post-retirement posts, and allegations of misconduct, as when cash was found at Justice Yashwant Varma's residence (March 2025); after an in-house inquiry and a removal motion, he resigned in April 2026.
  • Transparency builds trust: collegium resolutions have been published since 2017, and the CJI's office is a public authority under the RTI Act (Subhash Chandra Agarwal, 2019).
  • Necessary, not sufficient: independence also needs enough judges, infrastructure and speedy justice, because delay itself erodes faith in courts.

The statement is valid: without constitutionally guaranteed independence, rights, elections and federalism would depend on the goodwill of those in power. A transparent appointment process, timely filling of vacancies and credible self-regulation will keep the judiciary independent and accountable, the true guardian of constitutional democracy.

Article 39ALegal Services Authorities Act, 1987Section 12NALSA

Article 39A, inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), directs the State to provide free legal aid so that no citizen is denied justice because of economic or other disabilities, and the Supreme Court read the right to free legal aid into Article 21 (M.H. Hoskot, 1978; Hussainara Khatoon, 1979). The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, in force from 9 November 1995 (now National Legal Services Day), set up the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and a nationwide network of legal services institutions.

1. Who is entitled to free legal aid (Section 12)

  • Vulnerable groups: members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, women and children, persons with disabilities, and victims of trafficking or begar (Article 23).
  • Victims of undeserved want: such as mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster.
  • Industrial workmen and persons in custody, including in protective and juvenile homes and psychiatric hospitals.
  • Low-income persons: those whose annual income is below a ceiling fixed by the State government, or by the Union for cases in the Supreme Court.
  • Condition: the authority must be satisfied that the applicant has a prima facie case (Section 13); under NALSA's 2010 regulations an application must be decided within seven days.

2. Role of NALSA in rendering legal aid

  • Structure: the Chief Justice of India is Patron-in-Chief and a Supreme Court judge, by practice the next senior-most, the Executive Chairman; State, District and Taluk authorities and the Supreme Court Legal Services Committee implement its policies and schemes.
  • Legal aid and advice: through panel lawyers, front offices, legal aid clinics in jails and communities, and para-legal volunteers.
  • Public defenders: the Legal Aid Defense Counsel System provides full-time defence lawyers in criminal cases, on the public-defender model.
  • Lok Adalats: National, State and Permanent Lok Adalats settle disputes by compromise; their awards are final and free of court fees.
  • Awareness and victim support: legal literacy camps, and schemes for compensation to women victims of sexual assault (2018) and legal services to acid-attack victims (2016).

3. Assessment

  • Achievements: legal aid is now a statutory right, not charity; Lok Adalats cut cost and pendency, and public defenders help undertrials.
  • Low awareness: many eligible people do not know of their entitlement, and about three-quarters of prisoners are undertrials (Prison Statistics India 2022: 75.8%), most of them poor.
  • Quality concerns: low fees for panel lawyers, weak monitoring and little continuity breed the perception that free aid is poor aid.
  • Lok Adalat limits: many settlements involve petty or pre-litigation matters, and weaker parties may feel pressed to compromise.
  • Uneven capacity: State authorities differ widely in funds and staff.

NALSA has turned Article 39A into a working system. Better-paid and monitored lawyers, legal aid from the moment of arrest and sustained legal literacy can make access to justice real for the poorest, fulfilling the promise of equal justice.
free.upm-2023-gs3-1:
Manufacturing-led growthMSMEsPLI and National Manufacturing MissionFormalisation

Manufacturing contributes only about 17% of India's GVA, well short of the 25% target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011, although it is the sector best able to absorb surplus farm labour, raise productivity and earn exports. Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), defined under the MSMED Act, 2006, are its broad base: they produce about 30% of GDP and around 45% of exports, and are the largest non-farm employers.

1. Why manufacturing and MSMEs hold the key to faster growth

  • Moving labour out of farms: about 46% of workers are still in agriculture (PLFS 2023-24); factories offer higher productivity and wages, as the East Asian economies showed.
  • Linkages and scale: manufacturing pulls up mining, logistics, finance and services through strong backward and forward linkages.
  • MSMEs spread growth: they need little capital per job, work in small towns and clusters, and supply large firms as ancillaries.
  • Trade and resilience: domestic production of electronics, drugs and components cuts import dependence and taps China-plus-one supply chains.

2. Present policies of the Government (as of 2026)

  • Formalisation: Udyam registration (2020) links units to priority-sector credit and procurement preferences.
  • Prompt payment: since 2023, Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act lets buyers deduct payments to micro and small suppliers only if paid within the MSMED Act limit (at most 45 days), backed by TReDS and the MSME Samadhaan portal.
  • New entrepreneurs: term loans up to ₹2 crore for 5 lakh first-time women, SC and ST entrepreneurs (Budget 2025-26), and PM Vishwakarma (2023) for artisans.

3. Comment: results and gaps

  • Gains: PLI had brought over ₹2.5 lakh crore of investment and about 14.5 lakh jobs by June 2026 (DPIIT data), and India is now the second-largest mobile-phone maker.
  • Stagnant share: manufacturing's share of GVA has hardly moved in decades; PLI gains are concentrated in a few, often assembly-led, sectors.
  • Missing middle: over 99% of MSMEs are micro units (NSS 73rd round) that stay small and informal, with limited access to credit, technology and markets.
  • Cost disadvantages: logistics costs of 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT), costly power and land, and skill gaps reduce competitiveness against Vietnam and Bangladesh.

The policy direction is sound; what matters now is execution: cluster infrastructure, cheaper credit, skilling and labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, footwear and food processing, so that MSMEs grow into competitive firms and manufacturing-led growth creates jobs at scale.

Digital economyDigital Public InfrastructureDigital divideCyber security

Digitalisation is the use of digital technologies and data in production, payments, trade and governance. India's digital economy was 11.74% of GDP in 2022-23 (₹31.64 lakh crore) and is expected to reach nearly one-fifth of national income by 2029-30, growing almost twice as fast as the economy (MeitY report, January 2025). Its foundation is Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI): Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker and open networks.

1. Status of digitalisation (as of 2026)

  • Connectivity: 111.4 crore internet subscribers (TRAI, June 2026), cheap mobile data and 5G services since 2022.
  • Payments: UPI has handled over 20 billion transactions a month since August 2025, and over 95% of banking payment transactions are digital.
  • Welfare: Direct Benefit Transfer has moved over ₹52 lakh crore through 900+ schemes; 59 crore Jan Dhan accounts and DigiLocker (72 crore+ users) support it.
  • Commerce: ONDC, GeM, GST e-invoicing and the Account Aggregator framework bring small firms into formal markets and credit.
  • Jobs and services: the digital economy employed about 1.47 crore workers (2.55% of the workforce) in 2022-23, and India hosts about 55% of the world's global capability centres (PIB, 2025).

2. Problems faced

  • Digital divide: only 33% of women against 57% of men had ever used the internet (NFHS-5); rural, elderly, poor and disabled users lag behind, and content in Indian languages is still limited.
  • Cyber fraud: phishing, "digital arrest" scams and UPI frauds erode trust; the I4C's fraud-reporting system had saved about ₹11,158 crore by June 2026, a sign of the scale of the problem.
  • Privacy and security: the DPDP Act, 2023 is being phased in under its 2025 Rules, while attacks such as the ransomware attack on AIIMS Delhi (2022) expose weak cyber hygiene.
  • Exclusion by design: failed biometric authentication can deny rations or pensions, and many services lack offline alternatives.
  • Uneven adoption: most MSMEs and farmers use digital tools only for payments; two apps handle most UPI traffic, a concentration risk.

3. Suggested improvements

  • Last-mile access: complete BharatNet, expand PM-WANI public Wi-Fi and make devices affordable.
  • Skills: digital literacy through Common Service Centres and schools, with Bhashini tools for services in every language.
  • Trust: enforce the DPDP Act, CERT-In's six-hour incident reporting and the 1930 fraud helpline; build fraud analytics and grievance redress into every platform.
  • Beyond payments: use account-aggregator data for cash-flow credit to MSMEs, and ONDC and e-commerce exports for small producers.
  • Future capacity: data centres, AI compute (over 45,000 GPUs under IndiaAI by June 2026) and regular official measurement of the digital economy.

India's DPI model of "public rails, private innovation" has made it a digitalisation leader; closing the gender, rural and skill divides and building digital trust will turn this reach into broad-based productivity.

Corporate governanceMoral integrityProfessional efficiencyStakeholder trust

Corporate governance is the system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled, balancing the interests of shareholders, employees, customers, lenders and society. In India it rests on the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI's Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) Regulations, 2015. Two qualities make it work: moral integrity, which ensures that a company does the right thing, and professional efficiency, which ensures that it does things right.

1. Moral integrity in corporate governance

  • Meaning: consistency between stated values and actual conduct: honest accounts, fair dealing and refusal to bribe, mislead or cut corners, even when no one is watching.
  • Truthful disclosure: accurate financial statements and timely disclosure of material information, with auditors and independent directors acting as gatekeepers rather than rubber stamps.
  • Fairness to all stakeholders: no exploitation of minority shareholders, workers, consumers or the environment; related-party transactions need the approval of the audit committee and, when large, of shareholders.
  • Example: Johnson & Johnson's recall of about 31 million bottles of Tylenol in the US (1982), after tampering deaths, put consumer safety above profit. In India, the Tata Trusts, which own about two-thirds of Tata Sons, channel its dividends into philanthropy.

2. Professional efficiency in corporate governance

  • Meaning: competence, economy in the use of resources, timely decisions, innovation and sound risk management that create long-term value.
  • Effective boards: listed companies must have at least one-third independent directors and at least one woman director (Section 149), with audit and nomination committees and annual board evaluation.
  • Systems and controls: internal financial controls, a vigil mechanism for whistle-blowers (Section 177) and rotation of auditors (Section 139) prevent both waste and fraud.
  • Example: after the Satyam fraud (January 2009), a government-nominated board of eminent professionals stabilised the company and sold it through a transparent global bid to Tech Mahindra in April 2009, about three months after the fraud came to light, saving jobs and investor value. The Delhi Metro, under E. Sreedharan, completed its first phase ahead of schedule.

3. Why both must go together

  • Efficiency without integrity is dangerous: Wells Fargo staff opened millions of unauthorised accounts (exposed in 2016) to meet aggressive sales targets.
  • Integrity without efficiency is ineffective: honest firms that cannot compete or manage risk fail their employees and investors.
  • Strengthening both in India: CSR spending of 2% of average net profit by eligible companies (Section 135), the National Financial Reporting Authority (2018) for audit quality, the Kotak Committee (2017) reforms, and Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting for the top 1,000 listed companies from 2022-23.
  • Culture over compliance: codes of ethics, the "tone at the top", protection for whistle-blowers and executive pay linked to long-term, ethical performance.

Integrity without efficiency is weak and efficiency without integrity is dangerous. Ethical leadership that combines the two earns stakeholder trust, the most valuable capital a company has.

Official development assistanceConditionalityDignity of recipientsAid effectiveness

International aid, or official development assistance (ODA), is concessional finance, goods and expertise that donor countries and agencies give to poorer nations for development and humanitarian relief. The UN target is 0.7% of donors' GNI (1970). Its ethics turn on motive, means and outcome. OECD preliminary data show that aid fell by 23.1% in real terms in 2025, the largest annual drop on record, which makes these questions sharper.

1. Ethical basis of aid

  • Humanitarian duty: shared humanity obliges the well-off to prevent suffering when they can do so at modest cost, as Peter Singer argued in "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" (1972).
  • Global justice: colonial extraction and unequal trade rules give rich nations a historical responsibility; in climate finance, COP29 (Baku, 2024) set a goal of at least US$300 billion a year for developing countries by 2035.
  • Enlightened self-interest: pandemics, terrorism and forced migration cross borders, so aid that builds stability serves donors too.

2. Ethical concerns in contemporary aid

  • Strategic motives and conditionality: aid is often used to win votes, bases or markets; the structural adjustment conditions of the 1980s and 1990s were criticised for forcing cuts in health and education spending that hurt the poor.
  • Tied aid and debt: recipients may be required to buy from donor firms, or burdened with loans for projects of doubtful viability; Sri Lanka's Hambantota port, leased for 99 years to a Chinese company in 2017, became a symbol of "debt-trap" fears, though the label is debated.
  • Dependency and paternalism: donor-driven priorities can weaken local institutions and treat recipients as passive beneficiaries, not partners.
  • Misconduct and diversion: the Oxfam Haiti scandal (revealed in 2018) exposed sexual exploitation by aid workers, and corruption diverts aid from the needy.
  • Selfishness and unpredictability: rich countries pre-booked COVID-19 vaccines while COVAX struggled; in 2025 the US dismantled USAID, its aid fell by more than half, and all five largest donors cut aid, abruptly halting health and food programmes.

3. India's approach: development partnership

  • Demand-driven and without political conditions: India's South–South cooperation offers grants, lines of credit and training through ITEC (1964) on partners' priorities.
  • Examples: Vaccine Maitri (2021) supplied COVID-19 vaccines abroad; Operation Dost (Türkiye and Syria earthquake, 2023); about US$4 billion of support to Sri Lanka in its 2022 crisis; wheat and medicines to Afghanistan; Operation Brahma after the Myanmar earthquake (2025).
  • Self-scrutiny: partnership aid also serves strategic interests, so transparency and timely completion of projects matter.

4. Way forward

  • Aid effectiveness: the Paris Declaration principles of ownership, alignment, harmonisation, managing for results and mutual accountability.
  • Localisation and safeguarding: more funds through local organisations, codes against exploitation, and fair debt restructuring under the G20 Common Framework.

Ethical aid is a partnership, not charity: it respects the dignity and agency of recipients, keeps its promises and measures success by their development, not the donor's leverage.

Temple sculptureMedieval societyVisual social historyPerforming arts

Between the 8th and 16th centuries the temple was the hub of religious, economic and cultural life, and its walls were the largest canvas of the age. Built under the Chandelas, Eastern Gangas, Cholas, Hoysalas, Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara rulers, temples show gods and myths, but also kings, soldiers, dancers, merchants, couples and labourers. Read with inscriptions and travellers' accounts, these temple sculptures form a visual social history of medieval India.

1. Daily life, work and material culture

  • Occupations: friezes show herding, ploughing, carrying loads and craftsmen at work; the walls of the Sun temple at Konark (13th century) depict hunting, military processions and domestic life.
  • Dress and ornaments: the bracket figures (madanikas) of the Hoysala temples at Belur and Halebidu wear elaborate jewellery, girdles and hairstyles, a detailed record of contemporary fashion.
  • Trade and contact: the outer walls of the Hazara Rama temple at Hampi (Vijayanagara) show processions of horses, elephants and soldiers, and the nearby royal platform (Mahanavami Dibba) shows foreigners, probably Arabs or Persians, leading horses, a sign of the horse trade.

2. Women, family and leisure

  • Women's world: the surasundaris of Khajuraho (Chandela, c. 950–1050 CE) are shown applying kohl, looking into a mirror, writing a letter or removing a thorn from the foot.
  • Family and love: mother-and-child images and mithuna (loving couple) figures celebrate household life; the erotic panels reflect Tantric ideas and the belief that such images were auspicious.
  • Festivals: the dancing women and processions on the walls of the Hazara Rama temple recall the Mahanavami (Dasara) festival, which the Portuguese visitor Domingo Paes described.

3. Music, dance and the performing arts

  • Dance as worship: the gopurams of the Nataraja temple at Chidambaram carry the 108 karanas (dance poses) described in Bharata's Natyashastra.
  • Living traditions: dancing figures at the Kakatiya Ramappa temple (1213 CE, UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2021) helped Nataraja Ramakrishna revive the Perini dance in modern times.
  • Musicians: life-size female drummers and cymbal players stand on the roof of Konark's jagamohana (assembly hall).

4. Polity, war and religion

  • Kingship and war: the base friezes of Halebidu carry rows of elephants and horsemen, and other panels show kings and armies on the march.
  • Hero stones: virakals and sati stones, often set up near temples, honour warriors who died defending cattle or villages and record the practice of sati.
  • Devotion: the Chola temple at Darasuram narrates the lives of the Nayanar saints, showing the spread of Bhakti across social groups.

5. Limits of the evidence

  • Idealised images: sculpture shows courts, elites and the divine far more than peasants, labourers or the lower castes.
  • Canonical forms: many figures follow the shilpa shastras, so they must be read with inscriptions and literature.

Medieval temple sculptures are thus "history in stone": they show a hierarchical but vibrant society that worked, worshipped, fought and celebrated, and they remain a key source of social history alongside texts.
free.upm-2022-gs1-2:
Military disciplineAssured revenueDisunity of Indian powersSubsidiary alliance

From Plassey (1757) to the annexation of Punjab (1849), the English East India Company defeated nearly every major Indian power. Its armies were mostly Indian sepoys and often much smaller: at Plassey, Robert Clive had about 3,000 men against Siraj-ud-Daulah's 50,000. Victory came less from weapons than from organisation, finance and diplomacy: the Company fought as a disciplined, well-funded state against divided rulers.

1. Superior military organisation

  • Drill and discipline: sepoys were trained in European infantry drill, volley fire and formations such as the square, which could hold off the cavalry charges on which Indian armies relied.
  • Regular pay: the Company paid its standing army regularly in cash; many Indian armies, paid irregularly through chiefs, suffered desertions.
  • Unified command: a professional officer corps gave a clear chain of command; Indian armies were coalitions of contingents loyal to their own chiefs, which broke up when a leader fell.
  • Use of artillery: Indian rulers often had good guns, such as Tipu Sultan's rockets and the Sikh artillery, but rarely combined them with drilled infantry as the Company did.

2. Leadership, intelligence and diplomacy

  • Able leaders: commanders such as Clive, Eyre Coote and Arthur Wellesley chose the time and place of battle.
  • Divide and rule: the Company allied with the Nizam and the Marathas against Tipu in the Third Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92), and used the Peshwa's weakness to sign the Treaty of Bassein (1802).
  • Subsidiary alliance (1798): Lord Wellesley made rulers such as the Nizam pay for Company troops stationed in their States and disband their own forces, so Indian money financed the Company's army and disarmed its rivals.

3. Financial and naval strength

  • Assured revenue: after the Diwani of Bengal (1765), the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa paid for a large standing army; bankers such as the Jagat Seths backed the Company in 1757.
  • Sea power: command of the sea moved troops and supplies between the Presidencies and from Britain; no Indian power had a comparable navy.
  • Staying power: the Company lost battles, as at Pollilur (1780), but could keep fighting; for an Indian ruler one defeat was often fatal.

4. Weaknesses of Indian rulers

  • Disunity: there was no common Indian cause; the Marathas, Mysore, Hyderabad and the Sikhs fought one another, and Panipat (1761) had already weakened the Marathas.
  • Treachery and intrigue: Mir Jafar's troops stood aside at Plassey, and the Sikh commanders Lal Singh and Tej Singh are widely held to have betrayed their army in 1845–46.
  • Personalised reforms: Mahadji Scindia (with de Boigne) and Ranjit Singh modernised their armies, but the reforms decayed after them.

The Company's success was therefore organisational and political more than technological: a disciplined, regularly paid army, assured revenue, sea power and diplomacy overcame larger but divided forces. The same sepoys rose in 1857 when that bond of trust broke.

Constitutionalisation of environmentArticle 21Public interest litigationEnvironmental principles

The Constitution of 1950 said nothing explicit about the environment. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 48A (the State shall protect and improve the environment) and Article 51A(g) (a citizen's duty to protect it), but both are non-justiciable. The Supreme Court went further: by reading a healthy environment into the right to life under Article 21 and using public interest litigation (PIL), it turned environmental problems into enforceable constitutional rights. That is why many call it modern Indian law's most significant achievement.

1. How the Court constitutionalised the environment

  • Right to a healthy environment: in Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra (1985) the Court stopped limestone quarrying in the Doon valley; in Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991) it held that Article 21 includes the right to pollution-free water and air.
  • Absolute liability: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (oleum gas leak, 1987) made hazardous industries absolutely liable, without the exceptions of the English rule in Rylands v. Fletcher.
  • Principles made part of Indian law: Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum (1996) adopted sustainable development, the precautionary principle and polluter pays; Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) made chemical units in Bichhri, Rajasthan pay for the damage; M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) adopted the public trust doctrine.
  • Forests and climate: the T.N. Godavarman case (from 1995) protects all forests in the dictionary sense; in M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024), a case on the Great Indian Bustard, the Court recognised a right against the adverse effects of climate change under Articles 14 and 21.

2. Procedural innovations

  • PIL and relaxed standing: petitions by citizens such as M.C. Mehta brought the Kanpur tanneries polluting the Ganga (1987), the Taj Trapezium (1996) and Delhi's air (CNG for public transport, 1998) before the Court.
  • Continuing mandamus: the Court kept cases open for years and created expert bodies, such as the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority for Delhi (1998) and the Central Empowered Committee for forests (2002).
  • Specialised forum: the Court's call for environmental courts (A.P. Pollution Control Board v. M.V. Nayudu, 1999) and the Law Commission's 186th Report led to the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.

3. Why it is a major achievement

  • Rights where laws were weak: citizens can approach the Supreme Court directly when regulators fail.
  • A test for development: sustainable development and intergenerational equity became constitutional standards, giving future generations and wildlife a voice.

4. Limits of judicial environmentalism

  • Overreach: policy-making by courts strains the separation of powers, and judges lack technical expertise.
  • Implementation gap: after decades of orders, the Ganga and Yamuna remain polluted and Delhi's winter air is still hazardous.
  • Livelihoods: closure orders hurt workers and small units when no transition is planned.

The Supreme Court made the environment a constitutional value; strong regulators, the NGT and an executive committed to sustainable development must now carry it forward, rather than endless continuing mandamus.

Article 19(1)(d) and (e)Article 19(5)Reasonable restrictionsScheduled Tribes

Article 19(1)(d) guarantees every citizen the right to move freely throughout the territory of India, and Article 19(1)(e) the right to reside and settle in any part of it. Together they express single citizenship and one national market, without internal barriers. Yet these freedoms are not absolute: under Article 19(5) the State may impose reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public or to protect the interests of any Scheduled Tribe.

1. Scope of the rights

  • Internal freedom: citizens may travel, live and work anywhere in India; about 37% of Indians were migrants by place of last residence (Census 2011).
  • Only for citizens: foreigners do not enjoy Article 19.
  • Within India only: the right to travel abroad flows from personal liberty under Article 21 (Satwant Singh Sawhney, 1967; Maneka Gandhi, 1978), not from Article 19(1)(d).
  • Linked to livelihood: these rights make the freedom of profession and trade (Article 19(1)(g)) real for migrant workers.

2. Grounds and forms of restriction

  • Interests of the general public: public order, health, morals and security. In N.B. Khare (1950) the Court upheld externment under a public safety law with safeguards, and in Kaushailiya (1964) it upheld restrictions on the movement of sex workers on grounds of public health and morals.
  • Protection of Scheduled Tribes: the Inner Line Permit under the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation, 1873 (Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Mizoram and, since 2019, Manipur) and curbs on outsiders acquiring land in Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas protect tribal land and culture.
  • Public health and disasters: COVID-19 lockdowns (2020) under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897; quarantine and containment zones.
  • Public order: prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, 2023 (formerly Section 144 CrPC), curfews and externment of habitual offenders under State police laws.
  • National security: prohibited places under the Official Secrets Act, 1923, defence areas and border zones.

3. Other constitutional limits

  • Emergency: Article 358 suspends Article 19 during a national emergency declared on the ground of war or external aggression (44th Amendment, 1978).
  • Special provisions: Articles 371A (Nagaland) and 371G (Mizoram) protect customary law and land ownership; Article 16(3) lets Parliament prescribe residence requirements for some public jobs.
  • Judicial review: restrictions must be reasonable and proportionate; Anuradha Bhasin (2020) required prohibitory orders to be reasoned and proportionate.

4. Assessment

  • Justified limits: most restrictions protect vulnerable tribes, public health and security, and courts can review them.
  • Real barriers lie elsewhere: hostility to migrants, "sons of the soil" politics and domicile quotas in private jobs (Haryana's 75% law, struck down by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2023) restrict mobility more than law does.

The freedoms of movement and residence sustain fraternity and a common market. Restrictions are legitimate only when they protect the public or tribal communities and pass the test of proportionality.
free.upm-2022-gs3-1:
Public-Private PartnershipInfrastructure financingStation redevelopmentAmrit Bharat Station Scheme

A Public-Private Partnership (PPP) is a long-term contract in which a private partner finances, builds or operates a public asset and bears agreed risks, in return for user charges or payments from the government. India's infrastructure needs are huge: the National Infrastructure Pipeline (2019) projected about ₹111 lakh crore of investment for 2020-25, which budgets alone cannot fund. Railway stations, sitting on valuable urban land, are natural candidates for such partnerships.

1. Why PPP is required in infrastructure

  • Resource gap: public investment competes with health, education and welfare; private capital, along with asset monetisation (National Monetisation Pipeline, 2021), widens the pool of funds.
  • Efficiency: private firms bring design skills, technology and project management, and are rewarded for finishing on time.
  • Risk sharing: construction, operation and demand risks can rest with the party best able to manage them, as in the Hybrid Annuity Model (2016) for highways.
  • Life-cycle quality and value capture: a builder who also maintains the asset has a reason to build well, and land and footfall at stations or airports can earn revenue to cross-subsidise public facilities.

2. Role of PPP in redeveloping railway stations

  • The model: the developer upgrades the station and recovers its money from long leases of surplus railway land or air space for shops, offices and hotels.
  • Rani Kamalapati (Habibganj), Bhopal: redeveloped under the PPP model and opened in November 2021, with an airport-like concourse, modern passenger amenities and commercial development on railway land.
  • Gandhinagar Capital (2021): built through a joint venture of the Railways' station development company and the Gujarat government, with a hotel above the platforms.
  • A mix of models: for the largest stations the Government chose public funding instead, approving the redevelopment of New Delhi, Ahmedabad and Mumbai CSMT (about ₹10,000 crore) in 2022, while private partners take up commercial development and services.
  • Scale-up: under the Amrit Bharat Station Scheme, over 1,300 stations are being upgraded in phases; 103 were dedicated in May 2025 and 75 more in July 2026, taking the number of completed stations to 261.

3. Challenges

  • Land and heritage: encroachments, unclear titles and heritage buildings complicate plans.
  • Market risk: commercial land earns well mainly in big cities, so smaller stations cannot pay for themselves.
  • Affordability and coordination: user charges may burden poorer passengers, work must go on without stopping trains, and railways, city, metro and bus agencies must plan together.

4. Way forward: hybrid designs, with public money for the core station and PPP for commercial spaces, parking, retail and maintenance; balanced risk sharing and a renegotiation framework, as the Kelkar Committee (2015) urged; and multimodal hubs with metro and bus links planned under PM Gati Shakti.

Station redevelopment shows that PPP works best as a flexible partnership: private capital where commercial returns exist, public funding where they do not, both aimed at citizen-centric stations.
free.upm-2022-gs3-2:
Inclusive growthMarket economyFinancial inclusionJAM trinity

Inclusive growth is growth that is broad-based across sectors, regions and social groups, so that the poor share in its opportunities and benefits; the Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007-12) made "faster and more inclusive growth" its goal. In a market economy, prices and profits allocate resources. Markets create wealth efficiently but do not by themselves spread it fairly, so the answer lies in how markets and public policy work together.

1. Is inclusive growth possible under a market economy?

  • Yes, markets can include: after the 1991 reforms, faster growth, competition and cheaper goods and services lifted millions out of poverty; NITI Aayog estimated that multidimensional poverty fell from 24.85% (2015-16) to 14.96% (2019-21).
  • But markets alone exclude: people without assets, skills, credit or connectivity cannot take part, and growth led by capital- and skill-intensive sectors creates few jobs.
  • Market failures: private firms under-provide public goods such as health, schooling and rural roads, while information gaps and unequal bargaining power concentrate gains.
  • Hence markets plus the State: inclusion is possible when the State builds human capital, provides public goods and social protection and keeps markets competitive, as Kerala's social investments and the Nordic welfare states show.

2. Significance of financial inclusion for economic growth

The Rangarajan Committee (2008) defined financial inclusion as access to financial services and timely, adequate credit for vulnerable groups at an affordable cost.

  • Mobilises savings: PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) has over 59 crore accounts, about 56% held by women, turning idle household cash into deposits that fund investment.
  • Credit for enterprise: Mudra loans, Stand-Up India, PM SVANidhi and SHG–bank linkage finance micro-enterprises, farmers and street vendors, creating self-employment.
  • Formalisation and productivity: UPI and digital payments build credit histories, widen the tax base and cut transaction costs.
  • Efficient transfers: the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) has carried Direct Benefit Transfers of over ₹52 lakh crore through 900+ schemes, plugging leakages and freeing fiscal space.
  • Resilience and demand: insurance and pensions (PMJJBY, PMSBY, Atal Pension Yojana) protect households from shocks and sustain consumption.

3. Gaps that remain

  • Usage lags access: the RBI's Financial Inclusion Index rose to 70.0 in March 2026 from 67.0 a year earlier, but dormant accounts, low use of credit and insurance, gender gaps in usage and rising digital fraud remain.

Markets can deliver inclusive growth only when enabling public policy gives everyone the capabilities to take part. Meaningful financial inclusion, with credit, insurance and financial literacy, is one of its strongest levers.
free.upm-2022-gs4-1a:
Practical wisdomGoal displacementOutcome orientationGood governance

Wisdom, in the sense of practical wisdom (Aristotle's phronesis), is the ability to judge what really matters in a situation. An administrator absorbed in the periphery (formats, protocol, file notings, minor procedural lapses) while core issues such as delayed services, unresolved grievances and stalled projects wait, shows what Robert Merton (1940) called goal displacement: the means become ends. Such preoccupation largely defeats good governance, but a critical view shows that not all of the "periphery" is trivial.

1. Why officers get lost in the periphery

  • Defensive administration: fear of audit objections, vigilance inquiries and court cases makes officers protect themselves through procedure rather than solve problems.
  • Input-based appraisal: performance is judged by files disposed, meetings held and money spent, not by outcomes for citizens.
  • Visibility bias: ceremonies, VIP visits and reports are seen and praised; slow core work such as learning outcomes or maintenance is not.
  • Weak prioritisation: without clear goals and domain knowledge, every task looks equally urgent.

2. Why it leads to a travesty of justice (the case for agreeing)

  • Delay becomes denial: pensions, compensation and land records held up for a missing stamp or a spelling mismatch punish citizens for the system's errors.
  • Exclusion of the weakest: the poor, the elderly and the unlettered are least able to meet hyper-technical demands, so rigidity hits them hardest.
  • Misused time and resources: hours spent on trivial correspondence are taken from crises that are building up, such as disease outbreaks or stalled projects.
  • Accountability blurred: perfect files can hide failed outcomes; the officer is "compliant" while the scheme fails.

3. The critical view: the periphery is not always trivial

  • Procedure protects fairness: due process, recorded reasons and open tendering prevent arbitrariness and corruption (Article 14 and natural justice); ignoring them in the name of results breeds favouritism.
  • Small lapses can cause disasters: a skipped safety check or neglected maintenance can cost lives, so wisdom lies in knowing which detail is critical.
  • Context decides: a small error in a land record may decide a family's property; what is peripheral in one case is core in another.

4. Way forward: from rules to roles

  • Capacity building: Mission Karmayogi (2020) aims to move the civil service from rule-based to role-based functioning.
  • Outcome monitoring: PRAGATI (2015) and the Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) track results rather than inputs.
  • Simplification: self-attestation of documents and the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023, which decriminalised 183 provisions in 42 Acts, remove needless procedure.
  • Prioritisation tools: the Pareto (80/20) principle and the urgent–important matrix help officers focus on what matters.

Administration needs both rules and results, but rules must serve purposes. An officer with practical wisdom treats procedure as the servant of justice, not its master, and keeps the citizen's outcome at the centre: the essence of citizen-centric governance.
free.upm-2022-gs4-1b:
EmpathyCompassionEmotional intelligenceHumane administration

Intellectual competence (knowledge, analysis, judgement) tells a civil servant what is possible and lawful, and moral qualities (integrity, impartiality) tell him what is right. Empathy, the ability to understand a situation from another person's point of view, and compassion, the urge to act to relieve suffering, tell him what is humane. That is why the GS IV syllabus lists empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections among the foundational values of the civil service.

1. Meaning and place among civil-service attributes

  • Sympathy, empathy, compassion: sympathy is feeling for someone; empathy is feeling with them and seeing through their eyes; compassion adds the will to help.
  • Emotional intelligence: Daniel Goleman lists empathy as one of five components of emotional intelligence, with self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation and social skills.
  • Complement, not substitute: empathy without competence achieves little, and competence without empathy can be cold or even harmful.

2. How empathy and compassion help in crucial issues (illustrations)

  • Policies that fit real lives: understanding the life of a migrant worker produced One Nation One Ration Card, which lets families draw subsidised grain anywhere in the country.
  • Crisis management: during the COVID-19 lockdown (2020), district administrations ran shelters, community kitchens (as in Kerala) and transport for stranded migrants, decisions driven by compassion as much as by rules.
  • Winning trust: Armstrong Pame, an IAS officer in Manipur, built a road of about 100 km in Tamenglong district (2012), largely through public contributions, because villages there had no road.
  • Dignity for the needy: Kozhikode's Operation Sulaimani (2015), started by the district administration with hotel and restaurant owners, gave free meal coupons to the hungry without any questions.
  • Inclusive design: in Pragya Prasun v Union of India (April 2025) the Supreme Court held digital access to be part of the right to life and ordered KYC norms to be made accessible to acid-attack survivors and visually impaired persons; an empathetic officer can design for them without waiting for a court.

3. Critical decisions: compassion within limits

  • Fair, not partial: compassion must not become favouritism; it works through speed, dignity, guidance and lawful discretion, not by breaking eligibility rules.
  • Hard decisions made humanely: eviction, land acquisition or closure of polluting units may be necessary, but advance notice, rehabilitation and fair compensation make them just.
  • Avoiding compassion fatigue: constant exposure to suffering can numb officers; reflection, peer support and rest keep empathy alive.

Gandhi's talisman asks the decision-maker to recall the face of the poorest person he has seen and ask whether the step will help him. A civil servant who combines head and heart (competence, integrity and compassion) turns rules into humane governance.
free.upm-2021-gs1-1:
Bhakti movementVernacular literatureNirguna and sagunaComposite culture

Bhakti means loving, personal devotion to God. As a movement it began with the Tamil Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva) from about the sixth century CE, and spread to Karnataka, Maharashtra, and northern and eastern India between the twelfth and seventeenth centuries. Its saints sang in the people's own languages, so Bhakti literature became the foundation of many regional literatures and a strong force for social and cultural change.

1. Nature of Bhakti literature

  • In the mother tongue: saints composed in Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, Punjabi and Telugu rather than Sanskrit, ending the priest's monopoly over religious knowledge.
  • Oral and musical: it took the form of songs meant to be sung, such as padas, dohas, abhangas, vachanas and kirtans, and spread through singing gatherings and pilgrimages.
  • Two streams: nirguna poets such as Kabir, Ravidas and Guru Nanak worshipped a formless God and rejected idols and rituals; saguna poets such as Tulsidas, Surdas and Mirabai sang of Rama and Krishna in human form.
  • Egalitarian and critical: many saints came from artisan or "low" castes (Kabir a weaver, Ravidas a leather-worker, Namdev a tailor, Chokhamela a Mahar) and attacked caste pride, ritualism and hypocrisy.
  • Women's voices: Andal, Akka Mahadevi, Lal Ded and Mirabai expressed devotion as love, often defying social norms.

2. Contribution to Indian culture

  • Growth of regional languages: the Ramcharitmanas, the Jnaneshwari, Potana's Telugu Bhagavatam and Sankaradeva's works became classics that set the literary standard of their languages.
  • Social reform: by making every devotee equal before God, Bhakti weakened caste pride and priestly ritual; Basavanna's Anubhava Mantapa brought people of all castes together for discussion.
  • Religious harmony: Kabir addressed Hindus and Muslims alike, and the Guru Granth Sahib (compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604) includes verses of Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and the Sufi Baba Farid, a living symbol of composite culture.
  • Music, dance and art: Jayadeva's Gita Govinda inspired Odissi dance and Pahari painting; Purandara Dasa is called the father of Carnatic music; Sankaradeva's tradition gave the Sattriya dance; Narsinh Mehta's "Vaishnava Jana To" became Gandhi's favourite bhajan.
  • Popular culture: the Ramlila based on Tulsidas, the wari pilgrimage to Pandharpur and community kirtans keep these texts alive among millions.

3. Limitations

  • Caste survived: Bhakti did not abolish the caste system; many followings later hardened into sects or castes themselves.
  • Conventional roles: saguna poetry often reinforced conventional roles of submission even as it gave women a voice.

Bhakti literature democratised religion and language: it made the vernacular a medium of high thought, valued devotion over birth, and wove Hindu, Sufi and folk traditions into India's composite culture, a legacy carried forward by later reformers and the freedom movement.
free.upm-2021-gs1-2:
Bengal RenaissanceBrahmo SamajYoung BengalRationalism

The nineteenth-century socio-religious reform movements grew out of the encounter between Indian society and colonial rule. Western education, the printing press, missionary criticism and the rediscovery of ancient texts produced an English-educated middle class that questioned sati, caste, idolatry and the denial of education and remarriage to women. Bengal led the way in the Bengal Renaissance, through the Brahmo Samaj and the radical Young Bengal group.

1. Rise of the reform movements

  • Western ideas: rationalism, humanism and liberty, spread through English education, led reformers to test customs by reason.
  • Print and press: journals such as Ram Mohan Roy's Sambad Kaumudi (1821) carried reform debates to a reading public.
  • Defensive response: missionary attacks on Indian religions pushed reformers to purify their traditions from within.
  • Orientalist scholarship: the Asiatic Society (1784) and translations of the Upanishads gave reformers a classical basis for their arguments.

2. The Brahmo Samaj

  • Ram Mohan Roy: founded the Atmiya Sabha (1815) and the Brahmo Sabha (1828), later the Brahmo Samaj. Drawing on the Upanishads, he preached monotheism and opposed idolatry and priestly ritual; his campaign led to the abolition of sati by Bentinck's Regulation XVII of 1829. He also championed English and scientific education.
  • Debendranath Tagore: his Tattvabodhini Sabha (1839) and Tattvabodhini Patrika spread rational religion in Bengali.
  • Keshab Chandra Sen: took the Samaj into social reform (inter-caste marriage, widow remarriage, women's education) and beyond Bengal. Differences split it into the Adi Brahmo Samaj and Keshab's Brahmo Samaj of India (1866); the Native Marriage Act, 1872 legalised Brahmo-style marriages; and after Keshab married his under-age daughter into the Cooch Behar royal family, the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) was formed.

3. Young Bengal

  • Derozio: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio (1809–31), a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta, inspired by the French Revolution, taught his students to question everything.
  • Radical rationalism: Derozians such as Krishna Mohan Banerjee and Ram Gopal Ghosh attacked superstition, idolatry and caste, and championed women's rights, a free press, trial by jury and protection of ryots from zamindars.
  • Limitations: their open defiance of custom alienated orthodox society, they lacked a mass base, and the group faded after Derozio's dismissal and death in 1831. Yet Surendranath Banerjea later honoured them as the pioneers of modern civilisation in Bengal.

4. Growth across India

  • New organisations: Keshab's visit inspired the Prarthana Samaj (1867, Bombay; later led by M.G. Ranade), while the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873, Jyotiba Phule), Arya Samaj (1875, Dayanand Saraswati), Ramakrishna Mission (1897), the Aligarh movement and Sri Narayana Guru took reform to other regions and communities.
  • Wider social base: over time reform moved from upper-caste elites to the lower castes, and from religious doctrine to education and rights.

These movements created a modern, rational public sphere, improved the status of women and built the self-confidence that fed nationalism; their urban, elite base was their main limit.
free.upm-2021-gs2-1:
Constitutional moralityEssential facetsJudicial reviewConstitutionalism

Constitutional morality means fidelity to the core values and spirit of the Constitution (rule of law, liberty, equality, dignity, fraternity, and checks and balances), not merely to its text. Dr B.R. Ambedkar, drawing on the historian George Grote, told the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) that it "is not a natural sentiment. It has to be cultivated." The Supreme Court has turned the idea into a doctrine for testing laws, executive action and social practices against the Constitution's essential facets.

1. Meaning and essential facets

  • Rooted in the Constitution itself: its content comes from the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and the basic structure, so it is the morality the Constitution declares, not a judge's personal view.
  • Institutional facet: every organ of the State must respect its limits, constitutional conventions and the other organs, and must not act arbitrarily.
  • Rights facet: individual dignity and liberty must be protected even against majority opinion, which makes the doctrine counter-majoritarian.
  • Transformative purpose: the Constitution seeks to change an unequal society, so inherited customs are tested against equality and dignity.

2. Judicial decisions

  • Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014): the Court said constitutional morality means bowing to the norms of the Constitution and not acting arbitrarily; it advised the Prime Minister and Chief Ministers not to choose as ministers persons charged with heinous crimes or corruption.
  • Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018): a Constitution Bench asked constitutional functionaries to work in harmony and in the spirit of the Constitution, and held that the Lieutenant Governor is ordinarily bound by the aid and advice of the elected government.
  • Navtej Singh Johar (2018): decriminalising consensual same-sex relations under Section 377 IPC, the Court held that constitutional morality must prevail over social morality.
  • Joseph Shine (2018): the offence of adultery (Section 497 IPC) was struck down because it treated a wife as her husband's property, violating dignity and equality.
  • Indian Young Lawyers Association (Sabarimala, 2018): the majority held that excluding women aged 10–50 from the temple failed the test of constitutional morality; in 2019 wider questions of religious freedom were referred to a larger bench.

3. Criticism and limits

  • Vagueness: critics warn that an undefined standard can let judges substitute their own views for those of elected legislatures.
  • Pluralism: Justice Indu Malhotra's dissent in Sabarimala cautioned that in a pluralist society constitutional morality must also respect the freedom to practise one's faith.
  • Safeguard: the doctrine works best when applied with restraint and anchored in specific Articles and the basic structure.

Constitutional morality is the Constitution's conscience: it keeps power within limits and rights beyond the reach of passing majorities. Applied with judicial restraint and cultivated through civic education, as Ambedkar urged, it turns the text into living constitutionalism.
free.upm-2021-gs2-2:
Gender diversityHigher judiciaryCollegiumInclusive justice

Women are half of India's population, but few sit in the higher judiciary. From 1989, when Justice M. Fathima Beevi became the first woman judge of the Supreme Court, to 2021, only 11 women were appointed to it; the next, Justice V. Mohana, took oath only in June 2026, giving the Court two women judges with Justice B.V. Nagarathna. In February 2026 women held 116 of 781 sitting High Court judgeships (14.85%, Ministry of Law and Justice data).

1. Why greater representation is desirable

  • Diversity of perspective: judges' life experiences shape how they read facts and evidence; women judges add insight in cases of sexual violence, domestic abuse, custody, maintenance and workplace discrimination.
  • Equity: Articles 14 and 15(3) and India's commitments under CEDAW (ratified in 1993) call for substantive equality; an institution that guards equality should practise it.
  • Inclusiveness and public trust: a bench that mirrors society enjoys greater legitimacy, and women litigants, especially survivors of violence, may find courts more approachable.
  • Better jurisprudence: in Aparna Bhat v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2021) the Supreme Court set aside a bail condition requiring a man accused of molestation to have the complainant tie a rakhi on him, and told courts to avoid gender stereotypes; its Handbook on Combating Gender Stereotypes (2023) shows how such language can enter judgments.
  • Role models: women judges encourage women lawyers to stay in practice and seek elevation.

2. Why women remain few

  • A leaky pipeline: many women enter the district judiciary through competitive examinations, but elevation to High Courts depends heavily on senior advocates from the Bar, where women are fewer and are briefed less.
  • Opaque collegium: there are no published criteria or diversity goals, and the Memorandum of Procedure is still not finalised.
  • Age and seniority: women often become eligible late and get short tenures; Justice Nagarathna is in line to become the first woman Chief Justice of India in 2027, for about five weeks.
  • Workplace barriers: care responsibilities and few crèches or facilities in court complexes.

3. Measures

  • Diversity as a stated criterion: the collegium can consider women from both the Bar and the district judiciary and publish its criteria; former CJI N.V. Ramana (2021) backed women's demand for 50% representation.
  • Fair senior designation: transparent, points-based designation of senior advocates, as laid down in Indira Jaising v. Supreme Court of India (2017).
  • Support systems: crèches, flexible hours and safe infrastructure in courts.
  • Merit and diversity together: the pool of qualified women is now large, so diversity need not compromise merit.

Diversity on the bench is not tokenism but a condition of legitimacy: courts that decide questions of equality must reflect the society they serve. Progress such as four women serving at the same time as High Court Chief Justices (June 2026) and a second woman on the Supreme Court must become routine through a transparent and inclusive appointment process.
