Base year 2011-12GVA at basic pricesGDP at market pricesMCA-21 database

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. India's national accounts are compiled by the National Statistical Office (formerly the CSO), which periodically shifts the base year to reflect the changing structure of the economy. In January 2015 the base year moved from 2004-05 to 2011-12, and the method itself changed, bringing India closer to the UN System of National Accounts (SNA) 2008.

1. What is measured: factor cost to market prices

  • Before 2015: growth was headlined as GDP at factor cost, the income earned by the factors of production (wages, rent, interest and profits); sector-wise output was also valued at factor cost.
  • After 2015: sector-wise output is measured as Gross Value Added (GVA) at basic prices, which adds production taxes net of production subsidies, and the headline is GDP at market prices, which also adds product taxes (such as GST) net of product subsidies.

2. Data sources and coverage

  • Corporate sector: the old series relied on the RBI's sample studies of a few thousand companies; the new one uses the MCA-21 database of annual filings of lakhs of companies with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.
  • Establishment to enterprise approach: earlier, manufacturing value added was counted factory by factory from the Annual Survey of Industries and the IIP; now the whole enterprise is counted, including its head-office, marketing and other activities.
  • Financial sector: stock brokers, stock exchanges, mutual funds, pension funds and regulators such as SEBI, PFRDA and IRDAI were added, beyond banks and insurers.
  • Unorganised sector: an "effective labour input" method weights owners, hired workers and helpers by their productivity instead of treating all workers alike; local bodies and autonomous institutions are covered better.

3. Effects and debate

  • Higher growth: the new series raised growth for 2013-14 from 4.7% to 6.9%, at a time when credit, industrial output and exports were weak.
  • Criticism: experts questioned the quality of MCA-21 data (non-filing and shell companies), the use of single deflation and the gap with other indicators. In 2019 former Chief Economic Adviser Arvind Subramanian argued that growth had been overstated by about 2.5 percentage points; the Economic Advisory Council to the PM rejected this.

4. The latest revision (as of 2026)

  • Base year 2022-23 (released 27 February 2026): the new series uses double deflation for manufacturing and agriculture, supply and use tables, wider GST data, and direct estimates of the informal sector from the ASUSE and PLFS surveys. It puts nominal GDP about 3–4% lower than the old series, and growth for 2025-26 at 7.7% (provisional estimate, June 2026).

Each revision brings India's accounts closer to global standards. Regular base updates, timely surveys and transparent methods are essential for the credibility of statistics on which policy and investment depend.
free.upm-2021-gs3-2:
Annual Financial StatementRevenue budgetCapital budgetFiscal deficit

The Union Budget, called the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112, must show expenditure on revenue account separately from other expenditure (Article 112(2)). It is therefore divided into a Revenue Budget, covering the government's current receipts and day-to-day spending, and a Capital Budget, covering receipts and spending that change its assets and liabilities. The distinction shows whether borrowing is used to build assets or to meet running costs.

1. Capital Budget vs Revenue Budget

  • Effect on the balance sheet: revenue items neither create assets nor reduce liabilities; capital items do, for example building a road (asset) or repaying a loan (lower liability).
  • Nature: revenue items are recurring (taxes, salaries, interest), while capital items are mostly non-recurring and lumpy (borrowings, disinvestment, a new railway line).
  • Financing: revenue spending should ideally be met from revenue receipts; capital spending can justifiably be financed by borrowing, the "golden rule" of public finance.
  • Economic impact: capital spending adds to the economy's productive capacity and has a higher multiplier, while revenue spending supports current consumption and services.

2. Components of the Revenue Budget

  • Tax revenue: direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) and indirect taxes (GST, customs, excise); the States' share is passed on as devolution.
  • Non-tax revenue: dividends and profits from public sector enterprises and the RBI, interest receipts, fees, fines and grants.
  • Revenue expenditure: interest payments, salaries, pensions, subsidies (food, fertiliser, fuel), grants to States and the upkeep of defence. Interest alone is budgeted at ₹14.04 lakh crore in 2026-27 (BE).
  • Grants for assets: some grants to States create capital assets but are still shown as revenue spending; hence the effective revenue deficit, which subtracts them.

3. Components of the Capital Budget

  • Debt receipts: market borrowings (dated securities), treasury bills, small savings, provident funds and external loans.
  • Non-debt receipts: recovery of loans and disinvestment of government shares.
  • Capital expenditure: roads, railways, defence equipment, loans and advances to States and PSUs, investment in shares, and repayment of debt. Capital expenditure is budgeted at ₹12.22 lakh crore in 2026-27.

4. Deficits that link the two

  • Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts: borrowing for current spending.
  • Fiscal deficit = total expenditure minus revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts: the government's total borrowing need.
  • Primary deficit = fiscal deficit minus interest payments.

Since the revenue deficit (1.5% of GDP) is about a third of the fiscal deficit (4.3%), most borrowing now funds capital outlay. Shrinking the revenue deficit and protecting capital expenditure improves the quality of spending and keeps public debt sustainable.
free.upm-2021-gs4-1a:
Ethical performance matrixIntegrityImpartialityAccountability

A civil servant's performance cannot be judged by targets alone: how results are achieved matters as much as what is achieved. An ethical performance matrix plots an officer on a few observable traits and complements the output-focused APAR, which already asks the reporting officer to comment on integrity. The values written into the All India Services (Conduct) Rules in 2014 and the Second ARC's report on Ethics in Governance (2007) point to five such traits.

1. Five traits and why each belongs in the matrix

  • Integrity: honesty in money, decisions and words, and consistency between private belief and public action. It is the foundation: without it, every other strength, even competence, can be turned to private gain.
  • Impartiality and non-partisanship: decisions on merit and the same rules for all, whatever a person's caste, religion, wealth or political links. It gives effect to equality before the law (Article 14) and keeps citizens' trust when governments change.
  • Accountability and transparency: owning decisions, recording reasons and being open to audit, RTI and grievance review. It turns discretion into answerable power and deters misuse.
  • Empathy and compassion: sensitivity to the poor, the disabled, women and other weaker sections; the 2014 conduct rules expressly ask for responsiveness to the public, particularly the weaker sections. It makes rules humane and keeps the last person from being excluded.
  • Dedication to public service: commitment, diligence and moral courage, seen in timely delivery and in crises such as floods, elections and epidemics. It separates service from mere compliance.

2. Why a matrix rather than a single score

  • Traits balance one another: integrity without empathy becomes rigid; empathy without impartiality slides into favouritism; dedication without accountability can turn arbitrary.
  • Diagnosis, not only grading: plotting each trait separately shows where an officer needs training or mentoring, which fits Mission Karmayogi's competency-based approach (the Framework of Roles, Activities and Competencies, FRAC).
  • Evidence over impression: most indicators can be drawn from records, so the assessment depends less on one superior's opinion.

3. Safeguards in using it

  • Many sources: combine the reporting officer's view with peer and citizen feedback, as in 360-degree appraisal.
  • Fairness to the officer: entries must be communicated so that the officer can represent against them, as the Supreme Court held in Dev Dutt v Union of India (2008).
  • Reward courage: the matrix must credit officers who refuse illegal orders or take honest risks, not penalise them for friction with superiors.

Plotting performance on these five traits makes ethics measurable and moves the civil service from mere rule-compliance to values-based governance, in which the way a result is achieved counts as much as the result itself.
free.upm-2021-gs4-1b:
Foundational valuesCode of ethicsProbityPrevention of misconduct

An effective public servant needs, besides competence, foundational values that guide discretion where rules are silent. The UPSC syllabus, the Second ARC's report on Ethics in Governance (2007) and the values added to the All India Services (Conduct) Rules in 2014 identify them. Non-ethical behaviour, such as corruption, favouritism, apathy and abuse of power, can be prevented only when personal values are backed by institutional safeguards.

1. Ten essential values

  • These values reinforce one another: integrity without empathy becomes harsh, and empathy without impartiality becomes favouritism.

2. Why public servants slip

  • Discretion with weak oversight: complex procedures and face-to-face dealings create opportunities for rent-seeking.
  • Pressure and culture: political or peer pressure, fear of transfer and a cynical "everyone does it" culture.
  • Low risk of punishment: long delays in inquiries and prosecution weaken deterrence.

3. Ways and means: institutional and legal

  • Clear codes: a code of ethics stating values, besides conduct rules listing prohibitions, as the Second ARC recommended; declaration of assets and conflicts of interest; rotation in sensitive posts.
  • Anti-corruption law and agencies: the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, amended in 2018 to make bribe-giving a specific offence and to require prior approval (Section 17A) before probing decisions taken in official functions; the CVC; and the Lokpal (functional since 2019) and State Lokayuktas.
  • Transparency and technology: the RTI Act, 2005; e-procurement on GeM; direct benefit transfer and faceless tax assessment (2020) reduce discretionary contact.
  • Swift, fair consequences: time-bound inquiries; protection for those who report wrongdoing under the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004); premature retirement in public interest of officers of doubtful integrity after review (FR 56(j)).

4. Ways and means: personal and cultural

  • Values-based recruitment and training: the Ethics paper in the Civil Services (Main) Examination since 2013, foundation courses and Mission Karmayogi (2020).
  • Leadership by example: the "tone at the top"; seniors who model probity and protect honest juniors.
  • Reward honesty: fair appraisals, stable tenure through Civil Services Boards (urged in T.S.R. Subramanian v UoI, 2013) and recognition such as the Prime Minister's Awards for Excellence in Public Administration.
  • Citizen vigilance: social audits, citizens' charters, CPGRAMS and a free press make misconduct visible.

Values are the first line of defence and institutions the second. Ethical conduct lasts only when it is internalised and also enforced, combining character with compliance.
free.upm-2020-gs1-1:
Rock-cut architectureChaitya and viharaDonative inscriptionsAjanta murals

Rock-cut architecture means monuments carved out of living rock rather than built. In India it spans about a thousand years, from the Mauryan Barabar caves (3rd century BCE) to the monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora (8th century CE). As early timber buildings have perished, these caves, with their sculptures, paintings and inscriptions, are a prime source for Indian art and for early India's religion, polity, economy and society.

1. A record of artistic evolution

  • From wood to stone: the doorway of the Lomas Rishi cave at Barabar copies the curved front of a thatched hut, and the chaitya halls at Bhaja and Karle imitate wooden beams and ribs, preserving a timber tradition that has otherwise vanished.
  • Mauryan polish: the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves in Bihar, given to the Ajivika sect by Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha, have mirror-like polished walls.
  • Buddhist chaityas and viharas: Bhaja, Karle, Nasik, Kanheri and early Ajanta (2nd century BCE–2nd century CE) show the prayer hall and monastery maturing; Karle's is the largest rock-cut chaitya.
  • Classical climax: the later Ajanta caves (5th century CE), Elephanta (6th century), the Pallava rathas at Mamallapuram (7th century) and Ellora, where 34 Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves stand side by side.

2. A source for political history

  • Royal records: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription at Udayagiri (Odisha, c. 1st century BCE) records his campaigns year by year; Gautami Balashri's inscription at Nasik lists the victories of her son Gautamiputra Satakarni over the Shakas.
  • Dating dynasties: Varahadeva's inscription in Ajanta Cave 16 dates the later caves to the Vakataka king Harishena; Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh) inscriptions belong to Chandragupta II's reign.
  • Royal ideology: the Varaha panel at Udayagiri, Vishnu rescuing the Earth, is often read as an image of Gupta kingship; queen Naganika's Naneghat inscription records Satavahana Vedic sacrifices.

3. A source for economy and society

  • Trade and guilds: the caves cluster on Western Ghats routes linking ports such as Sopara and Kalyan with the Deccan; donor inscriptions at Karle, Nasik, Junnar and Kanheri name merchants, artisans, guilds (shreni) and Yavanas (foreigners).
  • Early banking: Ushavadata's Nasik inscription records deposits with weavers' guilds at Govardhana whose interest fed the monks.
  • Daily life: Ajanta's murals show palaces, dress, jewellery, music and ships alongside the Jataka stories.

4. A source for religious history

  • Hinayana to Mahayana: early chaityas centre on a plain stupa; later ones at Ajanta (Caves 19 and 26) carve the Buddha on it, marking the shift from symbol to image worship.
  • Puranic Hinduism and Jainism: Elephanta's three-headed Maheshmurti, Ellora's Ravana shaking Kailasa and the Jain caves of Ellora and Udayagiri–Khandagiri show new cults and their coexistence.

Few caves are precisely dated and donative inscriptions record merit rather than events, so they must be read with texts, coins and excavations. Still, they are history carved in stone, and conserving them (Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta are UNESCO sites) protects a primary archive of early India.
free.upm-2020-gs1-2:
Pala dynastyMahaviharasVajrayanaBuddhism in Tibet

The Pala dynasty, founded by Gopala around 750 CE when he was chosen king to end anarchy (matsyanyaya) in Bengal, ruled Bengal and Bihar for about four centuries. While Buddhism was fading elsewhere in India, the Palas were its last great royal patrons. Their mahaviharas made eastern India the intellectual centre of the Buddhist world, Vajrayana took mature form there, and teachers of the Pala age carried Buddhism to Tibet and beyond.

1. Royal patronage and the great monasteries

  • Vikramashila: founded by Dharmapala (late 8th century) near Bhagalpur in Bihar, it became the leading centre of tantric studies.
  • Somapura Mahavihara: Dharmapala's vast monastery at Paharpur (now in Bangladesh), one of the largest south of the Himalayas and a UNESCO site.
  • Odantapuri and Jagaddala: Odantapuri (Bihar Sharif) rose in the early Pala period; Ramapala founded Jagaddala in north Bengal in the late 11th century.
  • Nalanda revived: Devapala granted five villages to support a monastery built at Nalanda by the Sailendra king Balaputradeva of Suvarnadvipa (Sumatra), as the Nalanda copper plate records.

2. Doctrinal creativity: the Vajrayana phase

  • Vajrayana (Tantric Buddhism): liberation through mantras, mandalas, mudras, rituals and the guidance of a guru; female deities such as Tara gained importance.
  • Siddhas and literature: Mahasiddhas such as Saraha, Tilopa and Naropa composed mystical songs; the Charyapadas are among the earliest specimens of Bengali, Assamese and Odia.
  • Philosophy: Shantarakshita and his disciple Kamalashila of Nalanda combined Yogachara and Madhyamaka thought.

3. Spread beyond India

  • Tibet: Shantarakshita and Padmasambhava helped found Samye, Tibet's first monastery, in the late 8th century under King Trisong Detsen; Atisha Dipankara Srijnana of Vikramashila reached Tibet in 1042 and revived its monastic discipline, inspiring the Kadam school.
  • Two-way links: Atisha had studied under Dharmakirti of Suvarnadvipa (Sumatra); Pala manuscripts and bronzes reached Nepal, Tibet, Myanmar and Indonesia.

4. Art and manuscripts

  • Pala school of sculpture: images of the Buddha, Tara, Avalokiteshvara and Hindu deities in black stone and bronze, as in the Kurkihar and Nalanda hoards; Taranatha names Dhiman and his son Bitpalo as master artists.
  • Illustrated manuscripts: palm-leaf manuscripts of the Ashtasahasrika Prajnaparamita, with small paintings, are among the earliest surviving Indian miniatures.

5. Why this phase matters most, and how it ended

  • Final creative climax: Buddhism spread most widely within India under the Mauryas and Kushanas, but the Pala age was its last intellectual flowering and its bridge to Tibet.
  • Vulnerability: dependence on great monasteries and royal patrons, and tantric Buddhism's closeness to Hindu tantra, narrowed its popular base; after the Senas replaced the Palas, Turkish raids under Bakhtiyar Khalji (c. 1200) sacked Nalanda, Odantapuri and Vikramashila, and monks fled to Tibet and Nepal.

The Pala period thus turned Buddhism from a declining Indian faith into a pan-Asian tradition. Its scholarship, art and Vajrayana practice live on in Tibetan and Himalayan Buddhism, and in the revived Nalanda University (2014).
free.upm-2020-gs2-1:
Corrupt practicesSection 8AElection petitionPurity of elections

Under the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (RPA), corrupt practices (Section 123) such as bribery, undue influence and appeals on religion or caste can void an election. Yet unlike a conviction, which disqualifies automatically (Section 8), a finding of corrupt practice leads to disqualification only through a separate, multi-stage route under Section 8A, which the Election Commission of India (ECI) has long found slow and circuitous.

1. The present procedure

  • Finding by the court: an election petition is filed in the High Court within 45 days of the result (Section 81); the court names those guilty of corrupt practices (Section 99), and an appeal lies to the Supreme Court (Section 116A).
  • Reference to the President: the case must then be submitted to the President, within three months of the order taking effect, by an authority the Central Government specifies (Section 8A(1); the three-month limit was added by the 2009 amendment).
  • ECI's opinion binds: the President obtains the ECI's opinion and acts according to it (Section 8A(3)); the period of disqualification is decided case by case, up to six years from the date of the court's order.
  • Voting bar: the person is also barred from voting for the same period (Section 11A(2)); the petition for removal in Section 8A(2) now covers only disqualifications imposed before 1975.

2. Why simplification is needed

  • Delay defeats deterrence: petitions meant to be decided within six months (Section 86(7)) often outlast the House's term, so the guilty member serves most of it.
  • The Bal Thackeray case: the corrupt practices were committed in the 1987 Vile Parle by-election and upheld by the Supreme Court in December 1995, but the notification barring him from voting came only in July 1999, although the six-year period ran from December 1995.
  • An old complaint: the Law Commission's 244th Report (2014) records the ECI's 1998 concern over inordinate delays in these cases.
  • Unequal treatment: conviction disqualifies at once (Section 8; Lily Thomas, 2013 ended the shield for sitting members), and the ECI itself disqualifies for three years for not lodging expense accounts (Section 10A); a corrupt practice, which strikes at the purity of elections, takes the slowest route.

3. Arguments for caution

  • Natural justice and graded penalties: disqualification is a grave consequence and corrupt practices differ in gravity, so a hearing and the ECI's neutral opinion have value.
  • The real bottleneck is the slow trial of election petitions, not only the reference to the President.

4. Way forward

  • One decision: let the court fix the period while naming the guilty, after hearing the ECI, removing the separate reference.
  • Time-bound trials: dedicated election benches that keep to the six-month limit.
  • Clear norms: a minimum period for grave practices such as appeals to religion or caste (Abhiram Singh, 2017), and a deadline for the ECI's opinion.

The demand is justified: a penalty that arrives after the House's term has ended loses its force. One time-bound judicial process, with a fair hearing, would protect the purity of elections.
free.upm-2020-gs2-2:
RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019Information CommissionsSecurity of tenureInstitutional autonomy

The Right to Information Act, 2005 made the Central and State Information Commissions the final appellate authorities and gave them the security of constitutional bodies: a fixed five-year term (or up to age 65) and pay equal to that of the Election Commissioners. The RTI (Amendment) Act, 2019 amended Sections 13 and 16 so that the Central Government now prescribes the term, salaries and service conditions of all Information Commissioners, Central and State, raising concern about their autonomy.

1. What the amendments changed

  • Tenure: the fixed five-year term was replaced by a term prescribed by the Centre; the RTI Rules, 2019 set it at three years.
  • Pay and status: salaries are no longer linked to the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners (or, for State commissioners, to the Election Commissioners and the Chief Secretary) but fixed by central rules.
  • State commissions: the Centre now prescribes the service conditions of commissioners appointed by State governments.
  • Personal information: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Section 44(3), in force since November 2025 with the DPDP Rules) replaced Section 8(1)(j) with a blanket exemption for personal information, dropping the clause's own public-interest override.

2. The Government's case

  • Different nature: the Election Commission is a constitutional body (Article 324), while Information Commissions are statutory, so equal status was called an anomaly.
  • Rule-making gap: the original Act gave no power to frame rules on service conditions; the amendment was presented as streamlining.
  • Core intact: the right to information, time limits, appeals, penalties on officials, selection by a committee headed by the Prime Minister and removal only after a Supreme Court inquiry all remain.

3. Impact on autonomy and independence

  • Executive control: a body that decides appeals against ministries now depends on the executive's rules for its term and pay, and these can be changed without Parliament.
  • Lower stature: parity with Election Commissioners signalled that commissioners could direct the most senior officials; ending it weakens their authority.
  • Federal concern: the Centre fixes conditions for State commissions selected by State committees.
  • Wider secrecy: a blanket personal-information exemption may be used to refuse information on officials' conduct, assets or appointments.
  • Existing weaknesses magnified: vacancies and long backlogs already slow appeals; in Anjali Bhardwaj (2019) the Supreme Court ordered timely and transparent appointments, yet the Central Information Commission returned to full strength only in December 2025.

4. Way forward

  • Statutory security: restore a fixed term and status in the Act itself, beyond the reach of rules.
  • Cooperative federalism: leave State commissions' conditions to State laws or decide them with States.
  • Functioning commissions: fill vacancies on time, publish selection criteria, and enforce proactive disclosure under Section 4.

The amendments do not take away the commissions' powers, but placing their tenure and pay in executive hands weakens the independence on which RTI depends. Restoring statutory security, and a public-interest test for personal information, would keep RTI the master key to good governance, as the Second ARC (2006) called it.
free.upm-2020-gs3-1:
Intra-generational equityInter-generational equityInclusive growthSustainable development

Equity has two time dimensions. Intra-generational equity is fairness among people alive today, across classes, castes, genders and regions; it is the core of inclusive growth, which the Eleventh Plan (2007-12) made its goal. Inter-generational equity is fairness between the present and future generations. The Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development as development that "meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs".

1. Intra-generational issues: the inclusive-growth lens

  • Unequal access to jobs: growth led by capital- and skill-intensive sectors leaves about 90% of workers informal, and women's labour force participation was only 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Social and regional gaps: SCs, STs and backward districts lag in assets, learning and health; the Aspirational Districts (2018) and Aspirational Blocks (2023) programmes target these gaps.
  • Basic services: government health spending was only 1.43% of GDP and out-of-pocket spending 43.4% of health expenditure (National Health Accounts 2022-23), so illness pushes families into poverty.
  • Environmental injustice today: the poor bear most of the pollution, displacement by mines and dams, and climate shocks; the District Mineral Foundations (2015) and the Forest Rights Act (2006) try to share benefits with affected communities.

2. Inter-generational issues: the sustainability lens

  • Depleting natural capital: about 11% of groundwater assessment units are over-exploited, and Punjab extracts 156% of its annual recharge (CGWB, 2025); soils, forests and fisheries are also being run down.
  • Climate debt: today's emissions impose costs on future generations, which is why India has pledged net zero by 2070 and 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030.
  • Fiscal burden: high public debt and unfunded liabilities shift costs to future taxpayers; the FRBM Act, 2003 seeks to limit this.
  • Human capital: 35.5% of children under five were stunted (NFHS-5); undernourished children today mean a less productive workforce tomorrow.

3. How the two are linked

  • Trade-offs: free farm power and cheap coal help poor households now but deplete aquifers and the climate budget for the future.
  • Synergies: watershed works, rooftop solar, natural farming and green jobs raise incomes today while protecting resources.
  • Global equity: the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (Rio, 1992) links equity among nations to equity across time.
  • Better measurement: GDP ignores resource depletion; natural-capital accounts and the inequality-adjusted HDI show who gains and what is lost.

Inclusive growth without sustainability borrows from the future, and sustainability without inclusion is unjust today. Following the precautionary principle (Vellore, 1996) and the spirit of Mission LiFE, India must grow in ways that are fair to both.
free.upm-2020-gs3-2:
Potential GDPOutput gapTotal factor productivityStructural constraints

Potential GDP is the highest level of real output an economy can sustain over time when its labour, capital and technology are fully and efficiently used, without pushing up inflation. The difference between actual and potential output is the output gap: a positive gap signals overheating and inflation, a negative one signals idle capacity. The Economic Survey 2025-26 raised its estimate of India's potential growth from 6.5% to about 7%.

1. Determinants of potential GDP

Potential output follows a production function, Y = A × f(K, L):

  • Labour (L): the size of the working-age population, participation rates (especially of women), hours worked and the health of workers.
  • Capital (K): the rate of investment; India's gross fixed capital formation was 31.9% of GDP in 2025-26 (current prices, NSO, June 2026).
  • Human capital: education, skills and nutrition raise the quality of each worker.
  • Total factor productivity (A): technology, innovation, efficient allocation of resources, and institutions such as contract enforcement and the rule of law.
  • Enablers: infrastructure, energy, logistics, natural resources and macroeconomic stability.

2. Factors inhibiting India from realising its potential

Real GDP grew 7.7% in 2025-26 (NSO provisional estimates), close to the estimated potential; the challenge is to raise potential itself.

  • Under-used labour: women's labour force participation was only 41.7%, about 46% of workers remain in low-productivity agriculture (PLFS 2023-24), and about 90% are informal.
  • Skill and health gaps: poor learning outcomes, limited vocational training and child stunting of 35.5% (NFHS-5) lower future productivity.
  • Weak private investment and costly capital: the twin balance-sheet problem (bank gross NPAs peaked at 11.2% in March 2018) held back credit for years, and the Survey flags a high cost of capital.
  • Infrastructure and logistics: logistics costs of 7.8–8.9% of GDP (NCAER–DPIIT), costly power and slow land acquisition raise costs.
  • Narrow industrial and research base: manufacturing is only about 17% of GVA, and R&D spending is just 0.84% of GDP (2023-24).
  • Regulatory and judicial frictions: compliance burdens and slow contract enforcement deter firms from growing; the Jan Vishwas Act, 2023 began decriminalising minor offences.
  • Shocks: the COVID-19 contraction of 2020-21, global protectionism and climate extremes such as heat waves cut output and investment.

Closing these gaps can lift potential growth towards 8%, the pace needed for Viksit Bharat@2047. That requires second-generation reforms in land, labour, power, skills and the judiciary, not just demand stimulus.
free.upm-2020-gs4-1a:
Comprehensive National PowerHuman capitalSoft powerSocial harmony

Comprehensive National Power (CNP), a concept developed by Chinese strategists, measures a nation's total strength: not only its economy, armed forces and technology, but also intangibles such as the quality of its people, the appeal of its culture and the cohesion of its society. These intangibles rest on ethics and values. Honesty, discipline, compassion and tolerance turn a population into human capital, culture and policy into soft power (Joseph Nye's term), and diversity into social harmony.

1. Human capital: values make people productive

  • Work ethic and integrity: punctuality, diligence and honesty raise productivity and reduce the cost of supervision; trust between employers, workers and the state lowers the cost of every transaction.
  • Ethics of care in health and education: treating schooling (Article 21A) and public health (Article 47) as moral duties, not mere expenditure, builds a healthy and skilled workforce; Kerala's record in literacy and health shows the payoff.
  • Gender justice: equal opportunity for women brings half the nation's talent into the economy; female labour force participation of about 42% (PLFS 2023-24) shows how much is still lost.
  • Value-based learning: NEP 2020 places ethical and constitutional values in the curriculum, and Mission Karmayogi (2020) builds both competence and integrity in the civil service.

2. Soft power: credibility comes from values

  • Culture: yoga (the UN General Assembly declared the International Day of Yoga in 2014), the Buddha's message and Gandhian non-violence (2 October is the UN's International Day of Non-Violence) win admiration abroad.
  • Political values: a working democracy, pluralism and peaceful transfers of power make India's voice credible in the Global South.
  • Policies with a moral core: Vaccine Maitri (2021), Operation Dost after the Türkiye–Syria earthquake (2023) and the G20 presidency's theme of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (One Earth, One Family, One Future), during which the African Union became a permanent G20 member (2023), show power used for others.
  • Consistency: soft power evaporates when words and deeds diverge; keeping promises is its real currency.

3. Social harmony: values hold a diverse nation together

  • Fraternity: the Preamble's promise of fraternity and the duty to promote harmony (Article 51A(e)) turn diversity into strength rather than a fault line.
  • Tolerance and constitutional morality: respect for others' faith, language and customs prevents conflicts that drain security budgets and scare investors.
  • Social capital: trust and civic cooperation multiply the state's capacity, as when Kerala's fishermen rescued thousands of people during the 2018 floods.
  • Justice for the weak: fair treatment of weaker sections (Article 46) prevents alienation and extremism, which are the costliest threats to national power.

Tangible power can be bought or built quickly, but its intangible core grows only from values. A nation whose people are honest and capable, whose conduct abroad is principled and whose society is united possesses the most durable form of national power.
free.upm-2020-gs4-1b:
Holistic educationNEP 2020Critical thinkingSocial transformation

An injunction is a command: a list of dos and don'ts imposed from above and memorised for examinations. The statement holds that true education is the opposite, a pervasive process that develops the whole person (intellect, character, body and emotions) and, through such individuals, transforms society. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, approved on 29 July 2020 on the basis of the Kasturirangan Committee's draft, replaced the 1986 policy and largely shares this vision of holistic and multidisciplinary education.

1. All-round development of the individual

  • Strong foundations: the 5+3+3+4 structure brings pre-school (ages 3–6) into the system, and NIPUN Bharat (2021) aims at foundational literacy and numeracy for every child by Class 3.
  • Understanding over rote: experiential and inquiry-based learning, a curriculum reduced to its core essentials, and board examinations that test core competencies rather than memory.
  • No hard separations: between arts and sciences, curricular and extra-curricular activities, or academic and vocational streams; vocational exposure with internships begins in the middle stage.
  • Character and confidence: ethics, constitutional values, sports and arts, and teaching in the mother tongue wherever possible, at least till Class 5 (preferably till Class 8); a 360-degree holistic progress card replaces a marks-only report.

2. A tool of social transformation

  • Equity: special attention to Socio-Economically Disadvantaged Groups, a Gender-Inclusion Fund and Special Education Zones for disadvantaged regions.
  • Wider access: a target of 50% gross enrolment in higher education by 2035, multiple entry and exit points, and an Academic Bank of Credits.
  • Knowledge society: the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF Act, 2023) for research, and respect for Indian languages and knowledge systems.
  • Dignity of labour: the aim that at least half of all learners have vocational exposure by 2025 links learning with livelihoods.

3. Where practice still falls short (as of 2026)

  • Learning crisis: ASER 2024 found that only 23.4% of Class 3 children in rural government schools could read a Class 2 text, so the foundations remain weak.
  • Resources: public spending is still well below the policy's goal of 6% of GDP, and teacher vacancies and training gaps persist.
  • Exam culture: high-stakes entrance tests and coaching keep learning narrow and stressful, the very injunction-style education the policy rejects.
  • Federal concerns: some States object to aspects such as the three-language formula; the plan for one umbrella regulator in place of the UGC, AICTE and NCTE (the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, introduced in December 2025 and still before a Joint Parliamentary Committee as of October 2026) has raised concerns about autonomy.

NEP 2020 treats education as a transformative tool rather than an injunction. Its promise will be realised only when funding, trained teachers, assessment reform and cooperative federalism let classrooms practise what the policy preaches: learning for life.
free.upm-2019-gs1-1:
Gandhara schoolGreco-BactrianKushanasIndo-Hellenistic art

Gandhara art flourished in the north-west of the subcontinent (the Peshawar valley, Taxila, Swat and eastern Afghanistan) from about the first century BCE to the fifth century CE, reaching its peak under the Kushanas. The region lay on the Silk Road, where India met Bactria, Iran and Central Asia. Gandhara gave Buddhism some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form, expressing Indian themes in a Greco-Bactrian (Hellenistic) style for patrons from Central Asia.

1. Historical background

  • Greek legacy: Alexander's campaign (327–325 BCE), the Greco-Bactrian kingdom and the Indo-Greek kings such as Menander (Milinda) brought Hellenistic coins, cities and craftsmen to the north-west.
  • Central Asian rulers: the Shakas (Scythians), the Indo-Parthians (Gondophares at Taxila) and the Kushanas (from the Yuezhi of Central Asia) followed. Kanishka ruled from Purushapura (Peshawar) and patronised Buddhism.
  • Trade and contact: Silk Road commerce linked Gandhara with China, Central Asia and the Roman world, so Roman as well as Greek models reached its workshops.

2. Greco-Bactrian (Hellenistic) elements

  • Apollo-like Buddha: an oval face, straight nose, almond eyes and wavy hair gathered into a bun over the ushnisha recall the Greek god Apollo.
  • Drapery: a heavy, toga-like robe covers both shoulders and falls in thick, rhythmic folds, as in Greco-Roman statues.
  • Realism: careful modelling of muscles and anatomy; the Fasting Siddhartha from Sikri (Lahore Museum) shows every rib and vein.
  • Greek gods and motifs: Vajrapani appears as Herakles, and Hariti resembles the Greek Tyche; Atlas figures, garland-bearing cupids, acanthus leaves, Corinthian capitals, vine scrolls and Dionysian drinking scenes decorate stupas; one relief even shows the Trojan horse.

3. Central Asian elements

  • Costume of the steppe: donors and kings wear Scythian–Kushana dress, namely tunics, trousers, belts, cloaks and heavy boots.
  • Princely Bodhisattvas: Bodhisattvas are shown as Kushana nobles with turbans, moustaches and heavy jewellery; some Buddhas also have moustaches.
  • Iranian and Kushana royal symbols: the halo and the flaming shoulders seen on Kushana coins appear on Buddhas from Kapisa (Shotorak, Paitava).
  • Coins as a bridge: Kanishka's coins show a standing Buddha with the legend BODDO in Greek script, a Central Asian ruler honouring an Indian teacher in a Greek alphabet.

4. The Indian core

  • The themes, namely the life of the Buddha and the Jatakas, and the iconography (ushnisha, urna, long earlobes, mudras) remained Indian. Grey-blue schist, and later stucco, were the main materials; Mathura, under the same Kushanas, developed an indigenous style in red sandstone.

Gandhara was a true synthesis: a Hellenistic form with an Indian soul, made for Central Asian patrons. Through Bamiyan and the Silk Road it shaped Buddhist art in Central Asia, China and beyond, a symbol of India's cultural exchange with the world.
free.upm-2019-gs1-2:
Revolt of 1857Civil rebellionsTribal uprisingsSepoy mutinies

In the century between Plassey (1757) and 1857, British expansion provoked a long chain of resistance: civil rebellions of dispossessed rulers, zamindars and poligars; peasant and religious movements; tribal uprisings; and sepoy mutinies. The Revolt of 1857, which began at Meerut on 10 May 1857, gathered these scattered grievances into one great upheaval. It was their culmination, though it also went beyond them in scale and aim.

1. A century of local rebellions

  • Civil rebellions: the Poligar wars of the Tamil country (1799–1801), Velu Thampi's revolt in Travancore (1808–09), the Paika rebellion of Odisha (1817) and Kittur Chennamma's resistance (1824) were led by chiefs who had lost land and power.
  • Peasant and religious movements: the Sanyasi–Fakir rebellion in Bengal, the Faraizi movement of Haji Shariatullah and Dudu Miyan, the Wahabi movement and the Moplah outbreaks in Malabar mixed religious revival with anger against revenue, zamindars and moneylenders.
  • Tribal uprisings: the Kol (1831–32), Bhil and Khond risings and the Santhal hul (1855–56) of Sidhu and Kanhu resisted land alienation and outsiders (dikus).
  • Sepoy mutinies: Vellore (1806), over new dress rules seen as a threat to caste and religion, and Barrackpore (1824), over service in Burma, showed early discontent in the Company's army.

2. Why 1857 was their culmination

  • The same grievances, accumulated: heavy land revenue and evictions, ruined artisans, the Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur), the annexation of Awadh (1856) and fear of religious interference had built up for decades.
  • The same social groups: dispossessed rulers (Nana Saheb, Rani Lakshmibai, Begum Hazrat Mahal), zamindars (Kunwar Singh) and peasants joined the sepoys, who were largely peasants in uniform from Awadh.
  • The same form: like earlier risings, 1857 was led by traditional elites and sought to restore an older order, symbolised by the Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar.
  • Traditions of defiance: earlier risings had exposed British vulnerability, and the Santhal hul had been crushed only in 1856.

3. How 1857 went beyond them

  • Scale and unity: sepoys and civilians rose together across Delhi, Awadh, Rohilkhand, Bundelkhand, Bihar and central India, and Hindus and Muslims fought side by side.
  • A political aim: proclaiming Bahadur Shah emperor of Hindustan challenged Company rule itself, not just a local grievance.
  • Old limitations persisted: much of the south, Bengal and Punjab stayed quiet, many princes and the educated middle class stayed loyal, and there was no unified plan.

The Revolt of 1857 was thus both the climax of traditional resistance and a turning point: it ended Company rule (Government of India Act, 1858) and left a memory of united struggle on which modern nationalism later built.
free.upm-2019-gs2-1:
Separation of powersChecks and balancesArticle 50Basic structure

Separation of powers, theorised by Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), assigns law-making, execution and adjudication to separate organs so that no organ becomes tyrannical. The US Constitution applies it rigidly. India's Constitution does not: its parliamentary system fuses the executive with the legislature, and apart from Article 50 (separation of the judiciary from the executive) there is no explicit clause. It relies instead on a functional separation policed by checks and balances.

1. Why India does not follow strict separation

  • Fused executive and legislature: ministers must be members of Parliament (Article 75(5)) and are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)); the President is himself a part of Parliament (Article 79).
  • Executive law-making: the President and Governors issue ordinances (Articles 123 and 213), and much law is made through delegated legislation.
  • Judicial functions of the legislature: Parliament impeaches the President (Article 61), removes judges (Article 124(4)) and punishes breaches of privilege (Article 105).
  • Quasi-legislative role of courts: the Supreme Court frames its own rules (Article 145) and has issued guidelines where laws were silent, as in Vishaka (1997).
  • Judicial recognition: in Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) the Court held that India has not adopted the doctrine in its absolute rigidity, though the functions of the organs are sufficiently differentiated.

2. The core that is protected

  • Basic structure: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) counted separation of powers among the basic features; in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) the Court struck down Article 329A(4), by which Parliament had in effect decided an election dispute, a judicial function.
  • Mutual non-interference: legislatures cannot discuss a judge's conduct in the discharge of duties (Articles 121 and 211), and courts cannot question legislative proceedings for procedural irregularity (Articles 122 and 212).
  • Independent judiciary: security of tenure and salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund insulate judges from the other organs.

3. Checks and balances at work

  • Courts on the executive: in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) repeated re-promulgation of ordinances was held a fraud on the Constitution.
  • Parliament on the courts: after Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the First Amendment added Article 15(4) to permit special provisions for backward classes.
  • President on the Cabinet: the President may return the Cabinet's advice for reconsideration once (Article 74(1)) and return a Bill other than a Money Bill (Article 111).
  • Courts restraining themselves: in its opinion on the Presidential Reference (20 November 2025), the Supreme Court held that it cannot fix timelines for assent to Bills or deem assent, leaving room only for a limited direction in cases of prolonged inaction.

India therefore follows a separation of functions, not of persons: the organs overlap, but none may usurp another's core function. The balance rests on constitutional morality, with each organ exercising restraint and answering to the others.
free.upm-2019-gs2-2:
Article 323ACentral Administrative TribunalL. Chandra KumarJudicial independence

The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) was set up on 1 November 1985 under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, made under Article 323A, which the 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice. It was meant to relieve High Courts of service litigation by giving central government employees a quick, specialised forum. Four decades on, it functions much like a court: it tests rules against the Constitution, enforces orders through contempt and is held to standards of judicial independence.

1. Original design: a forum for service grievances

  • Jurisdiction (Section 14): recruitment and service matters of persons appointed to Union civil services and posts, members of the all-India services, and employees of bodies notified by the Union.
  • Simple procedure: it is not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure but by natural justice (Section 22); an application lies only after departmental remedies are exhausted (Section 20) and within a year (Section 21).
  • Mixed benches: judicial and administrative members bring together legal and service expertise.
  • Exclusive forum: Article 323A(2)(d) and Section 28 excluded all courts except the Supreme Court, and S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) accepted the tribunal as an effective substitute for the High Court.

2. How it now works as an independent judicial authority

  • Court-like powers: it can punish for contempt of itself like a High Court (Section 17), summon witnesses, call for documents and review its own decisions.
  • Constitutional adjudication: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that tribunals may test the validity of statutes and rules, except their parent Act, so the CAT strikes down service rules and promotion or seniority policies that violate Articles 14 and 16.
  • Binding the Union: its orders on transfers, penalties, pay and pensions bind ministries, and non-compliance invites contempt.
  • Independence standards: in R. Gandhi (2010) and the later Madras Bar Association cases, the Supreme Court required tribunals that replace courts to enjoy court-like independence in appointments and tenure; the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 created a National Tribunals Commission to oversee tribunal appointments and performance.

3. Limits on its independence and finality

  • Not the last word: after Chandra Kumar its decisions are open to a Division Bench of the High Court under Articles 226 and 227, which adds a tier and delays finality.
  • Executive control: the Department of Personnel and Training, a frequent litigant before the CAT, also handles its administration, budget and staff.
  • Vacancies and pendency: unfilled posts of members and short tenures slow disposal.
  • Narrow remit: it cannot hear challenges to its own parent Act, and many autonomous bodies remain outside its jurisdiction.

The statement is largely true: the CAT has grown from a grievance forum into a specialised court for service law. Timely appointments, administrative and financial autonomy and an effective National Tribunals Commission would secure its independence, while High Court review keeps it accountable.
free.upm-2019-gs3-1:
Goods and Services Tax101st AmendmentSubsumed taxesRevenue buoyancy

The Goods and Services Tax (GST), introduced on 1 July 2017 under the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016, is a destination-based tax on the supply of goods and services. The Union (CGST) and the States (SGST) levy it concurrently, with IGST on inter-State supplies (Article 269A). It subsumed 17 Central and State taxes and 13 cesses, replacing cascading "tax on tax" with input tax credit along the chain.

1. Indirect taxes subsumed in GST

  • Union taxes (8): central excise duty; additional excise duties on goods of special importance; additional excise duties on textiles; excise under the Medicinal and Toilet Preparations Act; additional customs duty (CVD); special additional duty of customs (SAD); service tax; and central surcharges and cesses on supplies.
  • State taxes (9): VAT or sales tax; central sales tax; purchase tax; luxury tax; entry tax in all forms; entertainment tax (except that levied by local bodies); taxes on advertisements; taxes on lotteries, betting and gambling; and State surcharges and cesses on supplies.
  • Kept outside: basic customs duty, alcohol for human consumption, five petroleum products (until the GST Council recommends otherwise), stamp duty and electricity duty; tobacco also bears central excise.

2. Revenue implications: the gains

  • Wider base, better compliance: invoice-matched credit, e-way bills (2018) and e-invoicing for large firms (2020) leave a digital trail that curbs evasion.
  • Buoyant collections: gross GST revenue excluding the compensation cess grew about 8.3% to over ₹22 lakh crore in 2025-26 (official data, April 2026), though less once the shrinking cess is counted.
  • Gains for consuming States: revenue follows consumption, helping populous consuming States.
  • Efficiency dividend: lower costs without cascading or check posts widen the base.

3. Revenue implications: the strains

  • Below revenue neutrality: the Arvind Subramanian committee (2015) suggested a revenue-neutral rate of about 15–15.5%, but rate cuts after 2017 kept the effective rate lower.
  • Compensation and the pandemic: States were guaranteed 14% annual growth over their 2015-16 revenue for five years (July 2017–June 2022). The COVID-19 shortfall was met by back-to-back loans of ₹1.1 lakh crore (2020-21) and ₹1.59 lakh crore (2021-22), repaid by extending the compensation cess.
  • Loss of fiscal autonomy: States cannot set rates alone, and the Union's one-third vote in the Council works as a veto.
  • Leakages: fake invoices, fraudulent credit claims and delayed refunds to exporters.
  • GST 2.0 (22 September 2025): two main slabs of 5% and 18%, plus 40% for luxury and sin goods, cut rates on many goods; the compensation cess, removed from most goods, ended on 1 February 2026, replaced by a higher central excise duty on tobacco and a new cess on pan masala.

GST has moved from teething troubles to a buoyant revenue base. Stable rates, quicker refunds, the dispute-settlement mechanism of Article 279A(11) and, in time, petroleum within GST would make it a truly "good and simple tax" for both levels of government.
free.upm-2019-gs3-2:
GDP growthFlexible inflation targetingJobs and investmentMacroeconomic stability

When this question was set in 2019, inflation was low but growth was slowing. By 2026 India had both: real GDP grew 7.7% in 2025-26 (new series, base 2022-23) and 7.8% in April–June 2026, while CPI inflation was 4.8% in August 2026, within the RBI's 4% ±2% band. Growth and price stability are necessary for a healthy economy, but not sufficient; jobs, investment, debt and resilience matter too. The view is therefore only partly valid.

1. Why the view has merit

  • Steady growth: under the new series, growth was 7.2% in 2023-24, 7.1% in 2024-25 and 7.7% in 2025-26 (provisional).
  • Anchored prices: flexible inflation targeting (RBI Act amended in 2016) has kept inflation lower and more stable than in 2009–13; the RBI cut the repo rate by 125 basis points in 2025 and raised it to 5.50% in October 2026 as inflation picked up.
  • Fiscal consolidation: the Union's fiscal deficit fell from 4.8% of GDP (2024-25) to 4.4% (2025-26 RE) and 4.3% (2026-27 BE), alongside capital spending of ₹12.22 lakh crore.
  • Healthier banks: the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and the 4R strategy cut banks' gross NPAs from 11.2% (March 2018) to about 2.3% (March 2025), reviving credit.
  • External buffers: record remittances of about US$135 billion (2024-25) cushion the current account.

2. Why growth and low inflation are not enough

  • Jobs: unemployment was 5.0% in September 2026 (PLFS, current weekly status), but about 46% of workers remain in agriculture (PLFS 2023-24), about 90% are informal, and women's labour force participation was only about 42% (PLFS 2023-24).
  • Food-price volatility: headline averages hide spikes; food inflation touched nearly 11% in October 2024, hurting poor households whose budgets are food-heavy.
  • Debt and interest: central debt is 55.6% of GDP (2026-27 BE), above the target of 50±1% by March 2031, and interest takes about a quarter of Union spending, crowding out health and education.
  • Private investment and manufacturing: public capex has done the heavy lifting, while manufacturing remains about 17% of GVA.
  • Distribution and risk: the post-COVID recovery was K-shaped, favouring formal firms and the better-off; dependence on imported crude (over 85%) and climate shocks to farming threaten stability.

3. What "good shape" requires

  • Employment-rich growth: labour-intensive manufacturing, MSME credit, skills and formal jobs for women.
  • Human capital: better learning and health outcomes to raise productivity.
  • Fiscal space and resilience: tax buoyancy, better quality of spending, energy transition and climate-proof agriculture.

India's macroeconomic fundamentals are sound, so the view is right about stability but incomplete. An economy is in good shape only when growth creates decent jobs and rising incomes for most citizens, not merely good headline numbers.
free.upm-2019-gs4-1a:
Nolan principlesPublic trustIntegrityAccountability

Public office is a public trust: power and public resources are held on behalf of citizens, never for personal gain. The UK's Committee on Standards in Public Life, chaired by Lord Nolan, set out in 1995 seven principles that apply to everyone holding public office, the Nolan principles. In India, the Second ARC's fourth report, Ethics in Governance (2007), and the values added to the All India Services (Conduct) Rules in 2014 rest on the same ideas.

1. The basic principles of public life

  • Wide application: the principles apply to elected representatives, civil servants and members of public bodies, and to private bodies when they deliver public services.
  • Beyond legality: they ask for conduct above the minimum that law demands; an act may be legal and still fail the test of selflessness or openness.
  • Indian echo: the 2014 amendment to the AIS (Conduct) Rules asks officers to uphold integrity, impartiality, accountability, transparency and responsiveness to the public, particularly the weaker sections.

2. Integrity, illustrated

  • Meaning: consistency between private values and public conduct, and freedom from improper influence.
  • Example: Satyendra Dubey, an engineer working as a project director with the National Highways Authority of India, reported corruption in the Golden Quadrilateral project to the Prime Minister's Office and was murdered in Gaya in November 2003. His sacrifice led to the CVC's PIDPI Resolution (2004) to protect whistle-blowers.
  • Lesson: integrity may demand personal risk, so institutions must protect those who show it.

3. Accountability, illustrated

  • Meaning: accepting responsibility for the results of one's office, not only for one's personal acts.
  • Example: Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned as Railway Minister in 1956, accepting moral responsibility for a rail accident at Ariyalur (then in Madras State), though he was not personally at fault.
  • Institutional form: the RTI Act (2005), CAG audits, parliamentary committees and social audits make accountability routine rather than exceptional.

4. Objectivity, illustrated

  • Meaning: decisions based on merit and evidence, applying the same rules to all.
  • Example: T.N. Seshan, as Chief Election Commissioner (1990–96), enforced the Model Code of Conduct firmly and even-handedly against candidates of every party, restoring public faith in elections.
  • Institutional form: merit-based recruitment through the UPSC, an independent constitutional body, keeps appointments free of patronage.

These principles turn public office into a public trust. Codifying them in a short code of ethics, as the Second ARC recommended, and practising them daily would strengthen citizens' trust in governance.
free.upm-2019-gs4-1b:
Public servantPublic dutyNeutralityCitizen-centric service

A public servant is a person who holds an office or performs a duty on behalf of the State, exercising public authority and paid from public funds for it. In law the term is wide: Section 2(28) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly Section 21 IPC) lists categories of public servants, and Section 2(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 goes further, covering anyone who performs a public duty, whatever the title of the post.

1. Meaning of the term

  • Legal sense: it covers civil servants, judges, police and armed forces officers, employees of local bodies and public-sector undertakings, and anyone authorised to perform a public duty.
  • Legislators included: the Supreme Court held a Chief Minister to be a public servant (M. Karunanidhi, 1979) and MPs to be public servants under the PC Act (P.V. Narasimha Rao, 1998); since Sita Soren (2024), legislators cannot claim parliamentary immunity for taking bribes.
  • Civil servant vs public servant: civil servants, governed by Articles 309–311, are a subset; every civil servant is a public servant, but not every public servant is a civil servant.
  • Ethical sense: the word "servant" signals that power is held in trust for the people; the citizen is the master, not a supplicant.

2. Expected role of a public servant

  • Guardian of the Constitution: upholding fundamental rights and the rule of law, and refusing illegal orders, so that governance follows the Constitution rather than personal or partisan will.
  • Neutral and continuous: governments change, but a non-partisan service implements every elected government's lawful policies faithfully and preserves institutional memory.
  • Welfare of the weak: Article 46 directs special care for the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections; the public servant is often their only link to the State.
  • Responsive and courteous: citizens' charters, Right to Services Acts and grievance portals such as CPGRAMS expect time-bound, polite service.
  • Problem-solver: Armstrong Pame, an IAS officer, built about 100 km of road in Manipur's Tamenglong district (2012) largely through public contributions, showing initiative within the law.

3. Values that make the role possible

  • Integrity and impartiality: the 2014 amendment to the AIS (Conduct) Rules lists integrity, impartiality, accountability, transparency and responsiveness, particularly to the weaker sections.
  • Empathy and dedication: compassion for the poor and diligence in crises separate service from mere compliance.
  • Accountability: to law, superiors, courts, audit and, above all, citizens.

The public servant is a trustee of public power. Moving from rule-based to role-based working, as Mission Karmayogi (2020) seeks, makes the service truly citizen-centric.
